results.title: Rent Out a GPU Server on Vast.ai: Rates, Costs, Utilization
highlights:
## The formula

```
gross = market rate ($/h) × GPU count × utilization × 730 h
yours = gross × your share after the platform's margin
power = (rented kW × utilization + idle kW × (1 − utilization)) × 730 h × electricity price
net = yours − power

```

Rented kW is the cards' rated power × 1.3, the system factor: CPUs, RAM, NVMe, fans and PSU losses draw power alongside the cards. The NEOXIS server, with eight RTX PRO 6000s, confirms it: about 6.5 kW at the data center's meter with all eight cards at full load, against 4.8 kW of rated card power - a factor of about 1.35. Idle kW is what the machine draws with nothing running. On the same server that is about 1.1 kW, roughly 790 kWh a month before anyone rents it (measured, neoxis.ai).

...

## What rates actually did: nine weeks of the market

GetDeploying publishes an open dataset of GPU rental prices across dozens of providers, with weekly medians going back a year (license: CC BY 4.0). Here is the median across providers per GPU-hour, on-demand, for the weeks starting on these dates:

| GPU | 3 Aug | 17 Aug | 31 Aug | 5 Oct | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B200 | 6.64 | 6.79 | 6.01 | 6.79 | +2% |
| H200 | 4.29 | 4.48 | 4.40 | 4.63 | +8% |
| H100 | 3.38 | 3.38 | 3.32 | 3.49 | +3% |
| RTX PRO 6000 | 2.21 | 2.19 | 2.20 | 2.20 | 0% |
| A100 | 1.87 | 1.76 | 1.76 | 1.85 | −1% |
| RTX 5090 | 0.58 | 0.46 | 0.63 | 0.70 | +21% |
| RTX 4090 | 0.44 | 0.45 | 0.42 | 0.44 | +1% |
| RTX 3090 | 0.22 | 0.13 | 0.17 | 0.22 | 0% |

Median across providers, on-demand, USD per GPU-hour; each week starts on the date shown. Source: GetDeploying, GPU rental price history (CC BY 4.0). The selection of cards is ours.

## The one interesting thing in that table

The RTX 5090 rose 21% in nine weeks. Nothing else moved like it – not its own sibling the 4090 (+1%), not the previous generation 3090 (back where it started), and not the data center cards, which moved between −1% and +8%.

But look at what else changed. In the week of 3 August, 8 providers listed the 5090; in the week of 5 October, 18 did. A median across providers moves when providers join or leave, not only when someone reprices – so part of that 21% may be about who is selling, not what they charge. Nor was the path a straight line: the 5090 dipped to $0.46 in mid-August before it climbed.

Two honest caveats. Nine weeks is a short window – four data points cannot separate a trend from a fluctuation. And these are advertised prices: GetDeploying counts every priced listing not marked sold out, which is not the same as capacity anyone actually rented at that price.

...

So instead of a single answer, here is the same machine at three utilization levels. 8× RTX 5090, median rate $0.703/h for the week of 5 October – the unrounded figure behind the 0.70 above – 730 hours, 75% host share, electricity at $0.15/kWh, 5.98 kW when rented (8 × 575 W × 1.3) and 1.1 kW idle:

| Utilization | Gross | Your share | Power | Net |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 100% | $4,106 | $3,079 | $655 | $2,424/mo |
| 60% | $2,463 | $1,847 | $441 | $1,406/mo |
| 30% | $1,232 | $924 | $281 | $643/mo |

results.title: Cheapest Monthly GPU Rental 2026: A100 & H100 Price Comparison
highlights:
What does a month of GPU rental actually cost in September 2026? For an A100 80GB running all 720 hours, the range runs from about $317 on Vast.ai’s marketplace (from $0.44/hr, if that rate held all month) to about $2,225 of hourly billing at Paperspace — with ApexVPS’s dedicated flat monthly rental at $1,290. For an H100 80GB, the span is roughly $1,433 (RunPod Community Cloud) to $2,369 (Lambda on-demand), with ApexVPS flat at $1,990. Every figure below is a public list price with a linked source, and every monthly equivalent is a simple 720-hour multiplication.

Two things matter beyond the raw number: whether the price is fixed (a flat monthly invoice) or variable (marketplace hours that reprice constantly), and whether the machine is dedicated and guaranteed or interruptible. We flag both on every row.

## A100 80GB: one month, every major option

| Provider | Rate (A100 80GB) | Month of 720 h | Model |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vast.ai | from $0.44/hr (PCIe) | from ≈ $317 | Marketplace hours; prices update hourly; interruptible hosts |
| RunPod (Secure Cloud) | $1.39/hr | ≈ $1,001 | Per-second billing from a prepaid balance |
| TensorDock | from $1.42/hr | from ≈ $1,022 | Marketplace/on-demand hours |
| ApexVPS | $1,290/month flat | $1,290 — fixed | Dedicated server; unlimited usage; no meter; crypto, no KYC |
| Vultr | ~$2.40/hr | ≈ $1,728 | On-demand hourly VM |
| Lambda | $2.79/hr | ≈ $2,009 | On-demand hourly |
| Paperspace | ~$3.09/hr | ≈ $2,225 | On-demand hourly |

Public rates checked September 2026 (sources below). “From” marketplace rates assume the cheapest listed host stays available and unchanged for 720 hours — a best case, not a quote.

## H100 80GB: one month, every major option

| Provider | Rate (H100 80GB) | Month of 720 h | Model |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RunPod (Community Cloud) | from $1.99/hr | from ≈ $1,433 | Community hosts; per-second billing |
| Vast.ai | ~$2.00/hr typical | ≈ $1,440 | Marketplace hours; $0.90–$2.27/hr by host tier |
| TensorDock | $2.25/hr (SXM) | ≈ $1,620 | On-demand hours |
| ApexVPS | $1,990/month flat | $1,990 — fixed | Dedicated server; unlimited usage; no meter; crypto, no KYC |
| RunPod (Secure Cloud PCIe) | $2.89/hr | ≈ $2,081 | Per-second billing from a prepaid balance |
| Lambda | $3.29/hr | ≈ $2,369 | On-demand hourly |

Public rates checked September 2026 (sources below). Marketplace “typical” rates vary by host and move hourly.

## How to read these tables honestly

The cheapest sticker prices all come from hourly marketplaces, and they are real — for as long as the host stays listed, at that price, with the machine actually free. A 720-hour month at a marketplace rate is a theoretical floor: hosts get occupied, prices reprice upward, and interruptible instances can stop mid-run. The flat monthly rentals are the opposite trade: you pay more than the theoretical floor and in exchange the price, the machine and the terms do not move for the whole term.

Note what a flat rental includes that an hourly GPU rate does not: at ApexVPS the monthly price covers the whole dedicated server — vCPU, RAM, NVMe storage and a bandwidth allowance (4–12 TB depending on the plan) — while hourly GPU listings frequently meter storage and bandwidth separately.

## When hourly wins, when flat monthly wins

- Hourly wins for short jobs, experiments, weekend fine-tunes and anything interruptible: pay $3 for two hours of A100 and stop.
- Flat monthly wins when a GPU must run all month and the invoice must be known in advance: production inference, month-long training, research clusters on a grant budget.
- The break-even rule: divide the flat monthly price by the hourly rate. ApexVPS’s $1,290 A100 breaks even with a $2.79/hr Lambda rate at about 462 hours (64% of the month); the $1,990 H100 breaks even with a $3.29/hr rate at about 605 hours (84%).
- Tier matters: on H100, ApexVPS’s flat $1,990 undercuts even some hourly secure-cloud rates (≈$2,081 for RunPod PCIe over a full month).

...

Cheapest sticker price: a marketplace A100 at Vast.ai’s “from $0.44/hr” — if you accept host variance and interruptions. Cheapest fixed, dedicated, guaranteed price: ApexVPS’s A100 at $1,290/month and H100 at $1,990/month, unlimited usage, no hourly meter, payable in crypto with no KYC and a 30-day money-back guarantee. If that profile fits, the ApexVPS monthly GPU plans from $249 (T4, A100, H100) are the direct next step.

...

By sticker price, marketplace hourly rates win: Vast.ai lists A100 80GB from $0.44/hr (≈$317 per 720-hour month) and H100 around $2.00/hr (≈$1,440). Among fixed dedicated monthly plans, ApexVPS is the cheapest in this comparison: A100 80GB at $1,290/month and H100 80GB at $1,990/month, both with unlimited usage and no hourly meter.

results.title: CoreWeave Is Renting GPU Capacity to AWS. That Tells You Everything About the Current Cloud Market. | CloudSyntrix
highlights:
## Pricing: 30% to 60% Cheaper, With a Different Risk Structure

The pricing differential between neoclouds and hyperscalers is substantial. Lambda offers NVIDIA H100 instances at approximately $3.29 per hour, undercutting hyperscalers by roughly 23% for equivalent hardware. Broader market analysis puts the overall neocloud pricing advantage at 30% to 60% compared to hyperscaler equivalents, with neoclouds offering transparent pricing and long-term multi-year take-or-pay contracts rather than the complex variable pricing models hyperscalers use.

Nebius reports 20% to 25% lower total cost of ownership compared to hyperscalers, attributed to its infrastructure efficiency and custom designs. For enterprises running large-scale, sustained AI workloads where compute cost is a significant budget line, this pricing differential translates into material savings.

The pricing advantage comes with a different risk structure. Neoclouds fund their capital expenditure requirements primarily through debt secured by GPU assets rather than through the operating cash flows that hyperscalers use. CoreWeave has secured over $10 billion in debt including GPU-backed delayed draw term loans. This financial structure creates execution risk that hyperscaler infrastructure does not carry: a neocloud’s ability to deploy and maintain infrastructure is dependent on continued access to debt markets and GPU supply in ways that AWS and Azure are not.

...

The supply-constrained environment has produced a specific dynamic that complicates the competitive narrative: neoclouds have become critical swing producers, renting capacity to hyperscalers during periods when demand exceeds their internal supply. This is not a durable structural arrangement. As hyperscalers build out their own captive capacity, analysts expect neocloud pricing pressure to increase and re-leasing risk to grow.

results.title: The bill is increasing even though prices haven't been raised | What is actually happening with AWS, Azure, and GCP｜梟 〜GLEANINGS〜
highlights:
“AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud have not raised prices yet.”

This is a sentence that always comes up when talking about cloud costs since the beginning of 2026. And it is half true. As of September 2026, there has been no official announcement that the three companies have collectively raised the base prices for general-purpose compute or storage.

The other half is the problem. GPU reservation slots have already gone up twice. In May, Google doubled certain network fees in North America. And all three companies officially have a mechanism for Japanese users where “the list price is in dollars, but the billing is in yen.” As long as this mechanism exists, even if the providers do not raise prices by a single cent, the billed amount will increase if the yen continues to weaken.

...

### There is certainly no sign of a blanket increase in base prices

I checked the AWS pricing page and What's New, Microsoft's licensing notices and Partner Center announcements, and the Google Cloud pricing change notification page. I went through them all, and as of September 2, 2026, there is no official announcement that base prices for general-purpose compute and storage are being raised across the board.

In response to an inquiry from DatacenterDynamics, AWS replied, “AWS's commitment to not raise pricing on fixed pricing models like On Demand and Savings Plans remains unchanged.” This is a statement that their policy of not raising prices for fixed-price models like On Demand and Savings Plans remains unchanged. The price revisions Microsoft made in 2026 were for Microsoft 365 (SaaS), which is a separate matter from the Azure infrastructure. What is listed on the Google Cloud “Infrastructure Services and Pricing Updates” page is still the content of the revisions implemented in October 2022 and April 2023.

Up to this point, it is as is often said.

### AWS GPU reservation slots have already gone up twice

However, it is not the case that there are no price increases at all.

AWS has a menu called EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, which allows you to reserve GPU computing resources for a set period. This pricing page states the following:

“Reservation prices are updated regularly based on trends in supply and demand for EC2 Capacity Blocks. The current prices are scheduled to be updated next in October, 2026.”

They are updated regularly based on supply and demand, with the next revision scheduled for October 2026. In other words, this menu is designed with the premise that prices will fluctuate.

In fact, it has moved twice since the beginning of 2026. In January, the p5e.48xlarge equipped with NVIDIA H200 was revised from $34.61 to $39.80 per hour in most regions, and the p5en.48xlarge was revised from $36.18 to $41.61. In July, after initially being announced for July 1 and then changed to July 7, the revisions covered P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de. The P6-B300 is at a level of $14.04 per hour per accelerator.

The prices for January mentioned here are only the amounts after the revision as of January. Because it went up again in July, the p5e.48xlarge currently on the pricing page is $47.76 per hour. That is exactly a 20 percent increase from $39.80.

AWS does not publish these revision rates. Since they do not keep old prices, the figures of “15 percent” and “20 percent” are calculated by news organizations and technical blogs that kept records of the price lists before and after the revisions. They are simply separate calculation results lined up, such as the January revision being exactly 15 percent and the July P5 revision being exactly 20 percent. It is not that AWS said “we are raising prices by 15 to 20 percent,” and the new and old prices themselves mentioned above are also based on the records of the reporting side.

And one more point. There are no individual notifications for these revisions in AWS's What's New or on their blog. What exists is the fact that the pricing page has been rewritten and the next scheduled update notice appearing in small print on that page. Price increases are being carried out in a way that you cannot notice unless you go looking for them.

### In May, Google doubled the transfer via peering in North America

Google Cloud also has one officially announced price increase for 2026.

The scope is egress transfer for CDN Interconnect, Direct Peering, and Carrier Peering. The official Google page states, "Effective May 1, 2026, Google Cloud will implement pricing adjustments to the list prices for data transfer out through CDN Interconnect, Direct Peering, and Carrier Peering," and the list prices have changed as follows.

- North America: $0.04 to $0.08 per 1GiB (2x)
- Europe: $0.05 to $0.08 (60 percent)
- Asia: $0.06 to $0.085 (approx. 42 percent)

Caution is required here. What was increased was transfer via peering, not Cloud CDN itself or general internet-bound egress transfer. Those pricing pages have no 2026 revision notice, and the egress notice page still shows the February 2024 implementation. If you generalize it as "Google raised network fees," the story becomes broader than the facts.

Note that Google does not provide a reason for this revision. The notice only contains the implementation date, the scope, and the old and new prices. This differs from how AWS explains Capacity Blocks based on supply and demand.

To summarize, the base prices of the three companies have not moved. What is moving are the quotas for AI computing resources and specific network paths.

### For all three companies, the list price is in dollars, but the billing is in yen.

This is where the main point begins. For users in Japan, there is actually a price hike that is having a more certain impact.

All three companies explain the same structure in their official documentation. The list price is set in US dollars, and billing is conducted in Japanese yen. The conversion rate is determined by each company using their own method.

...

### Even without price hikes, bills increase

Comparing the mechanisms of the three companies leads to the same conclusion. Even if cloud providers do not move their USD-denominated list prices by a single cent, the amount paid by Japanese users will increase if the Yen continues to weaken.

How much they have moved was covered in another article in this series. The Bank of Japan's reference foreign exchange rate has gone from 145 yen in July 2025 to 163 yen for the September 2026 application period. This is a weakening of the Yen by over 12 percent. This portion does not appear in any provider's price hike announcement, but it does appear on the invoice.

This is why the phrase "the three companies have not raised prices yet" is not a source of reassurance. Price hikes have already occurred in the form of exchange rates.

...

The next revision for AWS Capacity Blocks is scheduled for October 2026. If you are using GPU reservations, it is worth keeping this date in mind.

...

- As of September 2026, there has been no official announcement that AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud have generally raised base prices for general-purpose compute and storage.
- However, prices have risen in specific areas. AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML were revised twice, in January and July 2026, and the pricing page states that the next revision is scheduled for October 2026. AWS has not disclosed the revision rate, and the "15 to 20 percent" figure circulating is a value back-calculated from the old and new prices.
- Google Cloud raised prices for egress via CDN Interconnect, Direct Peering, and Carrier Peering starting May 1, 2026. In North America, the price doubled from $0.04 to $0.08 per GiB. Cloud CDN itself and general egress are not affected.
- For all three companies, the structure in Japan is that list prices are in dollars, while billing is in yen. Azure determines the rate based on the London closing price two business days before the end of the previous month, Google Cloud at the beginning of each month, and AWS at the time the invoice is created. The Japanese yen is not included in Google Cloud's currency fluctuation protection target currencies.
- Therefore, even if the provider does not raise prices, the billed amount will increase if the yen weakens. The standard foreign exchange rate has gone from 145 yen in July 2025 to 163 yen for the September 2026 application period.
- Domestically, Fujitsu will implement price revisions for FJcloud-V and others on October 1, 2026. The revision rates have not been publicly disclosed to that extent.
- In the State of FinOps 2026, 98 percent of organizations responded that they are managing AI spending (up from 31 percent two years ago), and SaaS spending management has reached 90 percent.
